title: Amortized GPU swapflow lab notes
content:
Objective:
- Explore how device<->host memory reclamation (what I'm calling 'swapflow') interacts with mixed-precision quantized (int8) model serving and KV-cache workloads.
- Measure amortized latency and tail inflation under realistic prompt lengths and bursty arrivals.

Hypothesis:
- When GPU memory pressure approaches a threshold (~70-85%), periodic background page-in/page-out events (CUDA UVM or driver-driven reclaim) produce short stalls that amplify p95/p99 even if average throughput is stable.
- Quantized models with persistent KV caches are especially sensitive because cache pages are large and rehousing them triggers multi-ms host->device transfers.

Environment / Setup:
- Cluster: local dev rig (for controlled repro) + Dedicated pool (staging)
  - Local: A6000 48GB, Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.1, pytorch 2.2 (custom build), nvcc info patched for pinned-host optimizations.
  - Staging: 4x A10G, multi-tenant but isolated queue for this test.
- Model: redwood-v1-7b-int8-kv (experimental quantized build)
- Runtime flags: kv-cache-enabled, continuous-batching=on, batching-window-ms=8, swap-threshold=0.75 (runtime policy for triggering device memory reclaim), prefetch-policy=deferred
- Workload: mixed prompts: 10% long (seq=2048), 40% medium (seq=1024), 50% short (seq=128). Inter-arrival: bursty Poisson with bursts (lambda spike) every ~60s.
- Tools: nvtop/nvidia-smi dmon, nvprof/nvtx markers in runtime, perf counters for memcpy H2D/D2H, p99 tracing via jaeger-like trace sampler, token-level latency from runtime logs.

Commands used (local):
- python run_bench.py --model redwood-v1-7b-int8-kv --batch 4 --mix-pattern bursty --seq-mix "2048:10,1024:40,128:50" --duration 900 --swap-threshold 0.75 --collect-traces
- nvidia-smi dmon -s u -d 5 > dmon-local.log &
- scripts/parse_traces.py dmon-local.log runtime-traces.json > swap_events.tsv

Metrics collected:
- mean_latency_tokens_ms (avg ms/token), p50/p90/p95/p99/p999 (end-to-end request), tail_uplift_pct (p99 / p50 - 1), throughput_tokens_per_sec, mem_host_used_mb, mem_gpu_used_mb, memcpy_h2d_rate_MBps (rolling), #device_swap_events/min

Observations (raw):
- Baseline run (swap-threshold disabled; same mix): p50 = 12ms, p95 = 65ms, p99 = 110ms, throughput ~ 28k tok/s.
- With swap-threshold=0.75: p50 = 13ms, p95 = 82ms, p99 = 138ms, throughput ~ 26.8k tok/s.
- Observed periodic step jumps in latency traces aligned with memcpy H2D spikes (avg 6-12ms blocked windows). These correspond to 1-3 large KV cache pages (4-16MB each) being streamed device-side.
- swap events/min measured: 0.7 (i.e., ~1 every 90s) under sustained 80% device mem util. In bursts, instantaneous rate spiked to 4/min.
- Amortized tail uplift (p99/p50) increased ~18% on staging runs compared to baseline.

Microtrace notes (nvtx):
- t=00:03:12: memcpy H2D spike (120ms window) caused 1.2s overall request slowdown for the concurrent long-chain generation; staging trace shows pipeline stalls instead of graceful stateless queuing.
- Follow-ups show that the runtime continued accepting requests into the batching window during the memcpy, which then see amplified latency once copy finished.

Quick hypotheses for root cause:
- Host->device DMA bursts triggered by page-in of evicted KV chunks cause synchronous stalls in the inference worker because the code path is using synchronous cudaMemcpy semantics for cache refill.
- The batching window allows work to pile up; when the memcpy completes and those requests try to access the KV cache, contention/locks in the cache manager cause serial stalls.
- Driver-level defragmentation / background GC could also be kicking in if we allocate pinned buffers dynamically; lack of pinned buffer reuse exacerbates copies.

Experiments attempted / short results:
1) Switch to async prefetch (cudaMemcpyAsync + stream-based events)
  - Implementation: runtime branch async-prefetch-2024
  - Result: reduced visible memcpy GIL in traces; p99 improved ~9% vs sync copy, but not fully eliminated.
2) Increase batching-window to 16ms (coalesce more)
  - Result: mean latency slightly up but p95/p99 lower during small bursts (tradeoff fits some SLAs).
3) Aggressive KV chunk pinning (pre-allocate pinned host buffers, reuse)
  - Result: memcpy throughput up, fewer driver-level page faults; p99 reduced further ~6%.
4) Reduce swap-threshold to 0.9 (i.e., allow higher device usage before reclaim)
  - Result: fewer swap events, but risk OOM on multi-tenant nodes; staging showed higher mean throughput when under 90% but one OOM happened during extended long prompts.

Quantitative run table (selected):
- Baseline (no swap): p50=12ms, p95=65ms, p99=110ms, tok/s=28,200, mem_gpu_avg=38GB
- swap-th=0.75 sync-copy: p50=13ms, p95=82ms, p99=138ms, tok/s=26,800, mem_gpu_avg=39.1GB
- swap-th=0.75 async-prefetch: p50=13.5ms, p95=74ms, p99=126ms, tok/s=27,100, mem_gpu_avg=39.0GB
- swap-th=0.9 pinned-bufs: p50=12.2ms, p95=69ms, p99=118ms, tok/s=28,000, mem_gpu_avg=40.4GB

Interpretation / quick conclusions:
- Swapflow (device<->host reclamation) is a real contributor to tail latency in quantized+kv workloads. The effect is multiplicative with batching and with synchronous cache refill semantics.
- Async prefetch + pinned host buffers significantly reduce the observable stall, but do not fully remove tail events because queueing semantics and lock contention still exist.
- Operational levers: raise swap threshold for Dedicated pools reserved for heavy KV workloads, favor pinned prefetch in runtime for these models, and tune batching-window dynamically during detected swap storms.

Open questions / next steps:
- Reproduce in a controlled multi-tenant scenario simulating eviction from other tenants (we only ran isolated staging so far).
- Profile lock contention in KV cache manager during bulk refill; consider sharded per-stream locks or lock-free refill strategies.
- Evaluate risk of higher swap-thresholds on memory fragmentation and OOM probability; run long-duration soak tests.
- Instrument driver/OS-level pagefaults to see if kernel-level reclaimers are involved (need dmesg/kernel logging enabled).
- Product impact: determine which SKU tiers (Hosted vs Dedicated) should get pin/prefetch/threshold defaults.

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Add NVTX markers to the cache fill path and instrument per-request wait time behind the KV lock.
- Add a mode to run workload with 'fake-evict' to force swap events at controllable times (tool: util/fake_evict.py).
- Sync with Maya and Hao next Tues to hand off async-prefetch branch for review.
- Draft a short runbook for SRE: if p99 shows periodic spikes correlated with memcpy, consider temporary policy of rejecting long prompts on that pool until pinned-prefetch lands.

Rough decision summary (for demo to PM):
- Short-term: enable pinned host buffer reuse + async prefetch for redwood-v1-7b-int8-kv in staging; monitor swap-events/min and p99.
- Mid-term: runtime changes to cache manager (reduce global locks, shard KV) and smarter batching backpressure during swap storms.
- Ops: expose swap-threshold config per-pool, default conservative for multi-tenant, aggressive for Dedicated.

Raw artifacts saved: swapflow-traces-20241105.zip, dmon-local.log, async-prefetch-branch.patch, fake_evict.py

Unresolved friction:
- Some memcpy spikes still line up with OS-level reclaim events; need kernel tracing to confirm.
- Risk profile of raising threshold on Dedicated without better isolation; need billing/contract review for SLA offsets.

End notes: this is intentionally a messy notebook. Prioritize reproducer (fake_evict) + small review of async-prefetch implementation.

-- julian
